prompt: Table 1 lists the melting point and boiling point of four substances. A substance is a liquid at temperatures above its melting point and below its boiling point. Which substance is a liquid at 50 °C?
explanation: Substance KLH-582 melts at 38 °C and boils at 118 °C. 50 °C is above its melting point and below its boiling point, so at 50 °C it is a liquid.

distractor_rationales.fault: it melts at 63 °C, so at 50 °C it has not melted yet and is still a solid
it boils at 46 °C, so at 50 °C it has already become a gas
it melts at 51 °C, just above 50 °C, so at 50 °C it is still a solid

real_world_check: A pure substance is a liquid at temperatures between its melting point and its boiling point, a solid below the melting point and a gas above the boiling point.

passage: Students squeezed a hand-warmer pack, Pack HL-2, to mix the chemicals inside. They taped a thermometer to the pack and read its temperature from 0 to 60 minutes.

graphic.caption: Temperature of Pack HL-2 after its chemicals were mixed

prompt: According to the graph, how did the temperature of Pack HL-2 change from 15 minutes to 35 minutes?
explanation: The points at 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 minutes are all at 52 °C. Over that stretch the line is flat, so the temperature did not change.

distractor_rationales.fault: the temperature falls only after 35 minutes, outside the stretch the question asks about
the temperature rises only during the first 10 minutes, before the stretch asked about
this describes the whole 60 minutes; from 15 to 35 minutes the line is flat at 52 °C

real_world_check: A chemical reaction can release thermal energy; the temperature holds steady while the energy released balances the energy lost to the surroundings, then falls as the reactants run out.
prior_free: MS-PS1-6 says reactions can release thermal energy, but nothing in it says when this invented pack stops warming or how long it holds steady; only the graph shows the flat stretch from 15 to 35 minutes.

passage: Students stacked identical Disc J-6 magnets on top of one another. For each stack, they counted how many identical steel washers the bottom of the stack could hold up in a hanging chain.

graphic.xLabel: Number of discs in the stack
graphic.caption: Washers held up by stacks of Disc J-6 magnets

prompt: Based on the graph, how does the number of washers held up change as more discs are added to the stack?
choices: It rises, then stays the same.
It drops, then it stays the same.
correct_answer: It rises, then stays the same.
explanation: From 1 to 4 discs the count climbs from 3 to 9 washers. From 4 to 8 discs it stays at 9 or 10 washers, so after the first few discs, more discs do not hold up more washers.

distractor_rationales.fault: the first four stacks climb from 3 to 9 washers, so the count does not stay level from the start

distractor_rationales.fault: no part of the cloud falls; the count climbs first, it never drops

real_world_check: For a stack of disc magnets holding steel, the pull grows as the stack gets longer at first, then extra discs far from the steel add very little, so the holding force levels off.
prior_free: MS-PS2-3 says magnet size affects magnetic force, but it does not say that adding discs stops helping, or after how many; only these counts show the level-off near four discs.

passage: Students made waves in a long tank of water. A paddle at one end moved the same way in every trial. Halfway down the tank, they placed one barrier at a time: Barrier G-4, Barrier JH or Barrier K-27. A sensor at the far end measured how tall the waves were after they passed the barrier. With no barrier, the waves there were 30 mm tall. With Barrier G-4, they were 12 mm tall. With Barrier JH, they were 24 mm tall. With Barrier K-27, they were 6 mm tall. A second sensor in front of the barrier showed that Barrier K-27 sent back the tallest waves toward the paddle.
prompt: Taller waves carry more energy. Which claim do these results support?
choices: Barrier K-27 let more wave energy pass than Barrier G-4.
Barrier JH let more wave energy pass than Barrier G-4 did.
Barrier G-4 sent more wave energy back than Barrier K-27 did.
Barrier JH sent back more of the wave energy than Barrier K-27 did.
correct_answer: Barrier JH let more wave energy pass than Barrier G-4 did.

refs.quote: With Barrier JH, they were 24 mm tall.
With Barrier G-4, they were 12 mm tall.

explanation: Behind Barrier JH the waves were 24 mm tall, and behind Barrier G-4 they were only 12 mm tall. Taller waves carry more energy, so more wave energy got past Barrier JH.

distractor_rationales.choice: Barrier K-27 let more wave energy pass than Barrier G-4.
distractor_rationales.fault: waves behind Barrier K-27 were 6 mm tall, shorter than the 12 mm behind Barrier G-4

distractor_rationales.choice: Barrier G-4 sent more wave energy back than Barrier K-27 did.
distractor_rationales.fault: the front sensor showed Barrier K-27 sent back the tallest waves of all

distractor_rationales.choice: Barrier JH sent back more of the wave energy than Barrier K-27 did.
distractor_rationales.fault: the front sensor showed Barrier K-27, not Barrier JH, sent back the tallest waves

real_world_check: A barrier reflects and absorbs part of a wave, so the wave that passes through is smaller, and a wave with a larger height (amplitude) carries more energy.

prompt: During a storm, Jun sees a flash of lightning far away. He hears the thunder from that same flash about five seconds later. Which statement best explains why he hears the thunder after he sees the flash?
choices: The thunder is made several seconds after the flash ends.
Light from the flash travels much faster through air than its sound does.
Sound starts out slow and speeds up as it moves along.
His eyes notice things faster than his ears do.
correct_answer: Light from the flash travels much faster through air than its sound does.
explanation: The flash and the thunder are made at the same moment. Light crosses the distance almost at once, but sound in air is far slower, so the thunder arrives seconds later.

distractor_rationales.choice: The thunder is made several seconds after the flash ends.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: thunder happens later than lightning; the heated air makes the sound at the same moment as the flash

distractor_rationales.choice: Sound starts out slow and speeds up as it moves along.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: sound changes speed as it travels; in still air of one temperature its speed stays about the same

distractor_rationales.choice: His eyes notice things faster than his ears do.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: the delay comes from our senses; the senses differ by a small fraction of a second, not five seconds

real_world_check: Light travels through air at about 300,000 km per second while sound travels at about 340 m per second, so the sound of a distant lightning flash arrives seconds after its light.

prompt: Hana makes waves by moving one end of a long rope up and down. Next, she keeps the same number of shakes each second, but she moves her hand twice as far up and down. Which prediction about the new waves is correct?
choices: The waves will reach the far end much sooner.
The waves will be spaced farther apart.
The waves will carry more energy along the rope.
The rope itself will travel along with the waves to the end.
correct_answer: The waves will carry more energy along the rope.
explanation: Moving her hand farther gives the waves a larger amplitude. A wave with a larger amplitude carries more energy. The shaking rate and the rope are the same, so the speed and spacing of the waves do not change.

distractor_rationales.choice: The waves will reach the far end much sooner.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: bigger waves travel faster; wave speed depends on the rope, not on the amplitude

distractor_rationales.choice: The waves will be spaced farther apart.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: amplitude sets wavelength; with the same shaking rate and the same rope, the spacing stays the same

distractor_rationales.choice: The rope itself will travel along with the waves to the end.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: a wave carries matter along with it; the rope only moves up and down while energy moves along it

real_world_check: The energy a wave carries increases with its amplitude, while its speed is set by the medium and its wavelength by speed and frequency.

passage: A space agency plans to land the same 10 kg probe on four planets. The planets differ in both mass and size. The table gives each planet's mass compared with Earth's and the weight the probe would have there.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Planet mass and the weight of one probe on each planet

prompt: How much more would the probe weigh on Planet Jorrin than on Planet Gavrel?
explanation: The probe weighs 141.0 N on Planet Jorrin and 62.0 N on Planet Gavrel. The difference is 141.0 N minus 62.0 N, which is 79.0 N.

distractor_rationales.fault: this subtracts the weight on Planet Kesset, the wrong planet
this subtracts the weight on Planet Halvic, the wrong row
this is the weight on Planet Jorrin alone, not the difference

real_world_check: The gravitational force on an object depends on the planet's mass and on the distance to the planet's center, so a larger planet with more mass can still give a smaller weight.
prior_free: Weight depends on a planet's mass and its size together, so no rule tells a student these invented planets' pull; the gap between Jorrin and Gavrel exists only in the table.

passage: Students timed how long Tablet GK took to dissolve in water. From trial to trial, they changed the water temperature, the form of the tablet and whether the water was stirred.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Dissolving times for Tablet GK

prompt: The students want to find out whether water temperature changes how fast Tablet GK dissolves. Which trial should they compare with Trial J-2?
explanation: Trial J-2 used a whole tablet in unstirred water at 20 °C. Trial HGLK-73 also used a whole tablet in unstirred water, but at 45 °C. Only the water temperature differs, so the two trials test its effect.

it changes both the temperature and the tablet form, so the effect of temperature cannot be separated

prompt: Based on the graph, which liquid has the least density?
explanation: Every sample had the same mass, 100 g. Density is mass divided by volume, so the liquid that takes up the most space for that mass is the least dense. Liquid GH-27 has the tallest bar.

distractor_rationales.fault: it has the shortest bar, so it packs 100 g into the least space and is the MOST dense; this reads small volume as low density

its 100 g takes up less space than Liquid GH-27, so it is denser

passage: Students tested how well three wraps keep hot water warm. The wraps were Wrap G-5, Wrap JK and Wrap L-18. First, they measured the mass of each empty steel cup, and all four cups were 150 g. prompt: Which quantity is the dependent variable in this investigation?
choices: the kind of wrap put around each cup
the mass of each empty steel cup
the starting temperature of the hot water

refs.quote: After 30 minutes, they recorded the final water temperature in each cup.

explanation: The students changed the wrap to see its effect. The quantity that responds to that change, and that they measured at the end, is the water temperature after 30 minutes.

distractor_rationales.choice: the kind of wrap put around each cup
distractor_rationales.fault: this is what the students changed on purpose, the independent variable

distractor_rationales.choice: the starting temperature of the hot water

real_world_check: In an investigation, the dependent variable is the outcome measured to see the effect of the variable the experimenter changes.

passage: Students rubbed two kinds of balloon, Balloon H and Balloon JL-6, on a wool cloth. They changed the number of rubs: 5, 10, 15 or 20. After rubbing, they slowly moved the balloon toward a strip of foil hanging from a thread. They measured the distance between the balloon and the foil when the foil first moved toward the balloon. The cloth, the foil strip and the room were the same in every trial. Table 1 shows the results.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Distance at which the foil first moved

prompt: According to Table 1, at what distance did the foil first move toward Balloon JL-6 after 15 rubs?
explanation: In Table 1, the row for 15 rubs and the column for Balloon JL-6 meet at 15.5 cm.

prompt: A magnet sits on a table. A steel paper clip slid toward it jumps to the magnet before the two touch. The magnet pulls steel clips but not bits of paper or foil, and it pulls just as well through a sheet of glass. What surrounds the magnet and pulls on the clip?
explanation: A magnet is surrounded by a magnetic field. The field reaches into the space around the magnet and pulls on steel without contact, even through glass, while paper and foil are not affected.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: magnetism is the same as static electricity; a charged object would also pull bits of paper, and this magnet does not
misconception: magnets pull by sucking in air; the pull works just as well through a glass sheet that blocks air
misconception: magnets attract by gravity; a small magnet's gravity is far too weak to move a clip, and gravity would pull paper too

real_world_check: A magnet is surrounded by a magnetic field that exerts forces on iron and steel objects without contact and passes through materials such as glass.

prompt: Lena rides her skateboard at 2 m/s. Later, she rides the same skateboard at 4 m/s. Her mass does not change. Which prediction about her kinetic energy at 4 m/s is correct?
choices: It will be twice as great as before.
It will stay the same, because her mass has not changed.
It will stay the same, because energy is conserved.
It will be four times as great as before.
correct_answer: It will be four times as great as before.
explanation: Kinetic energy depends on the square of speed. Doubling the speed from 2 m/s to 4 m/s multiplies the kinetic energy by 2 x 2, so it becomes four times as great.

distractor_rationales.choice: It will be twice as great as before.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: kinetic energy grows in step with speed; it grows with the square of speed, so doubling speed gives four times the energy

distractor_rationales.choice: It will stay the same, because her mass has not changed.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: kinetic energy depends only on mass; it also depends on speed

distractor_rationales.choice: It will stay the same, because energy is conserved.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: conservation means one object's energy cannot change; energy is conserved in total, but her kinetic energy rises as she speeds up

real_world_check: Kinetic energy equals one half of mass times speed squared, so doubling an object's speed makes its kinetic energy four times as great.

this divides Cord KH-5 by Cord HJ instead of by Cord L-30
this divides the tallest bar, Cord G-2, by the shortest, Cord HJ

real_world_check: At one shaking rate, wavelength is proportional to wave speed, and wave speed differs from cord to cord because it depends on the cord's tension and mass per length.

passage: Students tested four blocks made of different materials. They placed one block at a time inside an insulated box with a small heater. The heater ran for exactly 60 seconds for each block, so every block received the same amount of energy. Before heating, they found the mass of each block. After heating, they recorded how many degrees the temperature of the block had risen. Table 1 shows the results.

graphic.caption: Table 1. Mass and temperature rise of each block

prompt: Which block is made of the material that needs the greatest amount of energy to warm 1 g of it by 1 °C?
explanation: Each block got the same energy. Multiply mass by temperature rise: 1,500 for Block HL-71, 1,000 for Block K, 720 for Block JKL-508 and 1,200 for Block G-2. The same energy spread over the smallest number of gram-degrees means each gram-degree took the most energy, so Block JKL-508 is the answer.

distractor_rationales.fault: its mass times rise, 1,500, is the largest, so its material needs the LEAST energy per gram per degree
it had the largest temperature rise, and its mass times rise, 1,000, is larger than 720
it had the smallest rise only because it is so heavy; its mass times rise, 1,200, is larger than 720

real_world_check: When equal energy goes into different samples, the energy needed per gram per degree equals that energy divided by mass times temperature rise, so the smallest product marks the material that needs the most energy.

prompt: An analog signal changes smoothly, like a ramp. A digital signal is made of separate pulses, such as on and off, like steps. Which of these is an example of a digital signal?
explanation: A text message is sent as a code of separate on-off pulses, so it is a digital signal. The other three change smoothly, so they are analog.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: recorded sound on a disc is stored as pulses; a record groove is a smooth wavy copy of the sound, an analog signal
misconception: any electrical signal is digital; a basic microphone makes a voltage that rises and falls smoothly with the sound
misconception: a reading on a numbered scale is digital; the liquid rises and falls smoothly between the marks, which is analog

real_world_check: A digital signal encodes information as separate on-off pulses, as in text messages, while an analog signal varies smoothly, as in a record groove or a microphone's voltage.

prompt: Kenji heats white sugar in a pan. It turns into a liquid, then turns brown and then black. Steam and a sharp smell rise from the pan. After cooling, the pan holds a hard black solid that does not taste sweet. Which process made the black solid?
explanation: The black solid has new properties: a different color and no sweet taste, and it did not turn back into sugar when it cooled. New substances formed, so a chemical reaction took place.

distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: any change caused by heating is melting; melted sugar would cool back into sweet sugar, not a black solid
misconception: steam and smell mean the sugar simply evaporated; evaporation removes a liquid and cannot make a new black solid
misconception: heating can only change a substance's state; the solid that formed is a different substance, not sugar in another state

real_world_check: Strongly heated sugar breaks down into new substances, including black carbon-rich solid and water vapor, which is a chemical change because the products have new properties.

prompt: A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been on the same kitchen table all night. When Gina touches them, the metal spoon feels much colder than the wooden spoon. Which statement best explains this?
choices: The metal spoon is at a lower temperature than the wooden spoon.
Metal moves heat out of her hand faster than wood.
Cold flows out of the metal and into her hand.
Wood makes its own heat, while metal holds on to cold.
correct_answer: Metal moves heat out of her hand faster than wood.
explanation: After a night on the same table, both spoons are at room temperature. Her hand is warmer than both. Metal conducts heat away from her skin much faster than wood, so her skin cools faster and the metal feels colder.

distractor_rationales.choice: The metal spoon is at a lower temperature than the wooden spoon.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: an object that feels colder is at a lower temperature; both spoons sat all night in the same room and reached the same temperature

distractor_rationales.choice: Cold flows out of the metal and into her hand.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: cold is a thing that flows; heat flows from her warm hand into the cooler metal

distractor_rationales.choice: Wood makes its own heat, while metal holds on to cold.
distractor_rationales.fault: misconception: some materials make their own warmth or store cold; neither spoon produces heat

real_world_check: Objects left in the same room reach the same temperature, and metal feels colder than wood because it conducts heat away from the skin faster.
